tagline: From Tioga Pass, the highway drops more than three thousand feet
intro: The Lee Vining Canyon drive descends the Sierra Nevada’s steep eastern side, losing more than 3,000 feet in approximately 12 miles. It begins at Tioga Pass, 9,945 feet above sea level, and reaches US 395 at Lee Vining beside Mono Lake. This section of Route 120 is the Lee Vining Canyon Scenic Byway, a National Forest Scenic Byway administered by Inyo National Forest. The western approach to the pass is gradual; east of the summit, the road drops sharply toward the basin.

The wider Tioga Road crossing began in 1883 as a road to silver mines east of the pass and later became a private toll road. In 1915, Stephen Mather bought the road with his own money and donations from the Sierra Club and Modesto Chamber of Commerce, enabling public access through Yosemite’s high country. On the eastern approach, builders working along Lee Vining Canyon’s sheer walls in the 1930s faced the crossing’s most difficult construction.

From the pass’s stone entrance buildings, follow Route 120 toward Tioga Lake, a glacial lake beside the highway. Farther down, Lee Vining Creek drops from Ellery Lake into the canyon and continues toward Mono Lake. The road finishes at Lee Vining, at the eastern base of the Sierra.

moments.title: Tioga Pass
moments.text: Tioga Pass’s entrance buildings use heavy stone and logs at Yosemite’s eastern gateway. The ranger station dates to 1931 and the comfort station to 1934; Civilian Conservation Corps workers assisted with construction. Stone construction here set a precedent for other buildings in Yosemite’s high country. The ranger station sits into the hillside, with a porch across most of its front and massive timber window lintels. The log gates are replacements: after the original structures were removed, they were rebuilt in 1999 on surviving stone piers. The comfort station repeats the stone-and-log design, with sloping walls and a steeper roof.
moments.notice: Look for oversized stonework and heavy log framing at the ranger station’s porch.

moments.title: Tioga Lake
moments.text: Tioga Lake lies beside Route 120 just north of Yosemite’s Tioga Pass entrance, a small glacial lake within Inyo National Forest. Gaylor Peak rises above both the lake and the pass. Gaylor Peak’s summit consists of metamorphic rock, and the mountain is a fault block. Runoff from its eastern side drains into Tioga Lake, then feeds Lee Vining Creek and ultimately Mono Lake. The western drainage takes a different course, reaching Gaylor Lakes and the Dana Fork of the Tuolumne River. The lake’s high elevation and position near the pass make its weather unpredictable; frost is possible even in July.

moments.title: Lee Vining
moments.text: At the foot of the canyon, Lee Vining has carried several names. Chris Mattly laid out the town as Lakeview in 1926, but a post-office application revealed that another California town already used the name. Lee Vining was chosen in 1953, honoring Leroy Vining, who established a mining camp here in 1852. An earlier nickname, Poverty Flat, reflected the place’s unfavorable conditions for agriculture. The town stands on Mono Lake’s southwest shore, where tourism now supplies much of its economy. One local landmark is the Upside-Down House, built by silent-film actress Nellie Bly O’Bryan.

practical: Tioga Pass: Tioga Pass closes for winter snow. Opening and closing dates vary considerably from year to year. (checked 2026-10-11)
